newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Seita hit by new cancer suit.
newsitem.headline: France's Seita hit by new cancer suit.

text.p: The French tobacco giant Seita has been hit for the second time in a week by a lawsuit accusing it of causing a smoker's cancer, Seita and the lawyer for the smoker's family said on Thursday.

The latest suit, only the second legal case of its kind brought in France, was filed in the southern city of Beziers by the family of a young woman who died of lung cancer last October after smoking Gauloises Brunes cigarettes for over 20 years.
The suit said that Suzanne Berger of Servian, southern France, began smoking at the age of 13 and smoked 40 to 50 Brunes per day until she learned last year that she had cancer.
She had three children when she died, aged 35, a year after the initial diagnosis.
The family's lawyer, Francis Caballero, said the suit was intended to force Seita to inform the public of the health risks of its products.

The suit, which accuses the tobacco maker of selling an "inherently dangerous" product due to its addictive properties and its link to cancer, seeks more than one million francs ($200,000) in damages and interest.

A Seita spokeswoman said the latest suit, like a similar complaint brought against the firm last week, lacked serious legal grounds. She said similar suits filed outside France had never led to damages payments of any kind in the past.
In the earlier suit, also prepared by lawyer Caballero, a two-pack-a-day Gauloise smoker who is near death accused Seita of causing his cancer.
Richard Guerlain, 47, started smoking at age 14 and alleged that his cancer, too, was caused by smoking Seita's pungent Gauloises Brunes.
He is claiming 2.7 million francs ($513,000) in damages.
While a number of high-profile cases have been brought against tobacco companies in the United States, there have only been a handful in Europe.
Seita, which was privatised last year, said the only similar case ever filed in France was brought against a bank by the family of an employee who died.
The suit claimed she was the victim of passive smoking, but the court threw it out last month for lack of legal proof.
French cigarettes started carrying warnings about the health effects of smoking in 1976 and tobacco ads now are banned.
